query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid thermal processing, by providing an ultrafast heating and cooling cycle, kinetically freezes the mixed noble metal species into a single-phase high‐entropy alloy, because the fast decomposition of precursors minimizes atomic mobility that would otherwise lead to phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: A mixed precursor system comprising noble metal salts (or single‐source precursors) uniformly loaded onto a support (e.g., carbon) prior to thermal treatment.
generation.intervention: Switching from a conventional, slow heating (or fixed bed pyrolysis) regimen to a fast pyrolysis process (such as fast moving-bed pyrolysis) that applies ultrahigh heating and cooling rates during precursor decomposition.
generation.conditions: The synthesis is carried out under an inert or reductive atmosphere at high heating rates (and correspondingly high cooling rates) similar to those in fast moving-bed pyrolysis, with a direct comparison made against an otherwise identical process using a slow heating rate.
generation.structural_mediator: The limited atomic diffusion during the rapid thermal cycle results in a nuclei structure where the noble metal atoms are locked in an atomic-scale, homogeneous mixing, preventing elemental segregation.
generation.mechanism: Rapid heating induces simultaneous and nearly instantaneous precursor decomposition leading to a high supersaturation of metal atoms. The fast cooling limits diffusion and rearrangement, thus trapping the atoms in a metastable, single-phase high-entropy configuration. In contrast, slow heating permits differential reduction and substantial atomic mobility, resulting in phase separation or elemental segregation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized via fast pyrolysis will show a uniform, single-phase high-entropy alloy structure with homogeneously dispersed noble metals, whereas those formed under slow heating conditions will exhibit signs of phase separation and elemental segregation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced by conventional slow (fixed bed) pyrolysis methods that tend to show phase-separated structures due to extended atomic mobility during gradual heating.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy systems synthesized from similar single-source precursors where decomposition temperatures and reduction kinetics are comparable. It may not hold for systems with widely varying precursor decomposition profiles or where diffusion remains dominant even during fast processing.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative effect of rapid heating on phase homogeneity is supported, the exact threshold heating and cooling rates required and the magnitude of improvement in alloy uniformity have not been precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of noble metal precursor-loaded supports: one processed via fast pyrolysis (high heating and cooling rates) and one using slow, conventional pyrolysis, ensuring all other parameters (composition, atmosphere, support) are identical.
measurements: X-ray diffraction to assess phase purity
HAADF-STEM with EDX mapping to evaluate elemental homogeneity
Thermal analysis (e.g., DSC) to confirm rapid thermal profiles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fast pyrolysis sample does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in single-phase formation and elemental mixing compared to the slow-heated control (i.e., if both samples show similar degrees of phase separation), the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. It is demonstrated that the formation of HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles and the inhibition of precursor mobility during the formation process favors the formation of a single phase. The proposed formation principle is supported by simulations of the nanoparticle formation

cited_evidence.text: We carried out control experiments to verify the assumption that the strategy of pyrolysis reduction of mixed metal precursors governed the formation of alloys (Fig. 4). We took the ternary (NiPdPt@GO) alloy as an example to investigate the influence of different pyrolysis strategies on alloy formation, because more elements will make the characterization much more complicated and challenging. In the FMBP process, the NiPdPt alloy was formed without phase segregation (Fig. 4b). In contrast, as shown in Fig. 4d, when the propulsion speed was decreased to 1 cm s−1 (20 s for precursors to reach the heating zone), namely the slow moving bed pyrolysis (SMBP), the phase-separated NiPdPt nanoparticle was clearly formed, where Pt and Pd were not uniformly in the NiPdPt nanoparticles. More obviously, Pd only existed in the core of NiPdPt nanoparticles obtained by the conventional FBP strategy (923 K) with a heating rate of 20 K min−1 (~31 min from 298 K to 923 K), indicating a completely phase segregation (Fig. 4f, Supplementary Fig. 22).
